title: Direct, transparent democracy — where we stand
preamble: This platform never takes sides on the questions it asks. But it is not neutral about everything: it stands for a process. We believe residents should be able to see their government's money to the receipt, speak on its decisions directly, and check every count themselves. That stance — for participation itself — is the one position this platform holds openly, and this page shows the evidence behind it.

definitions.meaning: Residents speak for themselves — on paper, by phone, or in person — instead of being spoken for or polled by proxy. Direct does not mean binding: results here are signal, not command. Elected officials keep their authority and their responsibility; what changes is how clearly they can hear the county.

Every number cites its source. Every count shows its tier. Every gap is named. The platform's own books, costs, code, and activity log are as public as the budgets it maps — the standard points at us first.

The institutions this county already has — quorum court, city board, school boards — working with better information and demonstrated public support. This platform is furniture for that system, not a replacement for it.

tenets.claim: Direct participation is not an experiment — it is the oldest working form of local government.
tenets.evidence: New England towns have governed themselves by open town meeting since colonial times; Tocqueville marked their independence in 1831. Swiss citizens vote on roughly 15 issues a year, and more than a third of all national referendums ever held worldwide took place in Switzerland. The scale where this works best is exactly ours: small places where the issues touch everyone.

sources.label: Direct democracy at the local level in Switzerland (research)

tenets.claim: Taking part changes the people who take part — durably.
tenets.evidence: Stanford's deliberative polling research found that structured participation produced measurable knowledge gains and large, lasting effects on civic engagement — participants followed politics more closely and voted more, nearly a year later. Participatory budgeting studies report the same: residents who allocate public money once become more politically active afterward, and collaboration with community organizations raised turnout among groups that usually stay home.

sources.label: The lasting effects of deliberation on civic engagement (Stanford FSI)
Participatory budgeting and political participation (People Powered)

tenets.claim: Communities agree on more than their arguments suggest — when the platform doesn't reward fighting.
tenets.evidence: Taiwan's vTaiwan process — statements people could agree or disagree with but never reply to — repeatedly surfaced majorities hidden under loud disputes, and produced real regulation on ride-sharing and online alcohol sales. Washington, D.C. launched the same family of tools city-wide in 2025. The mechanics matter: no reply threads, no dogpiles, bridge-building scored above dunking. That is the deliberation design this platform inherits.

tenets.claim: Small governments can move real money when priorities are made visible.
tenets.evidence: Washington County, Wisconsin reallocated 15% of its operating budget through priority-based budgeting. Lahti, Finland ran city-wide participatory budgeting where anyone could vote at the library — and the budget doubled the next year because the pilot worked. Porto Alegre, the birthplace of participatory budgeting, saw improved roads, water, schools, and civic trust — and its later erosion when political commitment faded is exactly why we build durable public infrastructure rather than one-time campaigns.

sources.label: Porto Alegre: participatory budgeting and sustaining change (WRI)

tenets.claim: Transparency is what makes a count citable — and it has to start with us.
tenets.evidence: A number an official can cite must survive a hostile challenge: who was counted, how they were verified, what the arithmetic was. That is why every result here shows its tiers, every cell under 20 renders as a range, the vote path is one gate, and the activity log is hash-chained and publicly anchored so that not even the operator can quietly rewrite history. And it is why the sponsor's own books open before anyone else's are asked for: a standard you won't hold yourself to isn't a standard.

tenets.claim: Signal beats silence — and signal is not command.
tenets.evidence: The officials this county elects often already know what needs doing; what they lack is demonstrated public support that survives scrutiny. A verified count is political cover, not political pressure. This platform's results bind no one. They simply make it impossible to say nobody was asked — and, over time, awkward not to ask.

tradition.idea: Visiting New England, Tocqueville judged town institutions the schools where liberty is learned — self-government as a practice you acquire by doing, not a belief you're taught. A county that never asks its residents anything is a school with no classes.

Ostrom's field research demolished the assumption that communities can't govern shared resources without top-down control. Her design principles for institutions that endure read like this platform's spec: those affected participate in making the rules; monitoring is done by and answerable to the community; conflict resolution is cheap and accessible; and the community's right to organize is respected by higher authorities. A county budget is a commons; the platform is Ostrom's monitoring principle, built.

Bowling Alone documented two generations of collapse in American civic connection — league bowling down 40% while bowling itself rose; meeting attendance, committee service, and institutional trust all falling together. Pew finds three-quarters of Americans say trust in government is shrinking. The decline is the diagnosis; participation infrastructure is a treatment you can actually build.

counterarguments.answer: The most serious objection, and California's Proposition 8 is its proof case. Our answers are structural: results here bind no one — elected officials retain authority and legal responsibility; the charter's bright lines exclude the dangerous question types entirely (no candidates, no ballot measures, no named individuals); and questions are framed about process and money, not about groups of people. A signal system cannot strip anyone's rights; it can only make opinion visible — and deliberation mechanics are designed to surface cross-group consensus, not raw majority muscle.

counterarguments.objection: Money captures direct democracy — signatures and campaigns are bought.
counterarguments.answer: True in California's paid-signature industry. Here there are no signatures to buy and no campaign spending to out-shout: questions enter through a neutrality pipeline with wording review, and the research finding cuts the other way at mass scale — a whole electorate is far harder to lobby than a small body of officials. The platform also publishes who sponsors it and what it costs, so the money behind the microphone is never a mystery.

counterarguments.objection: Voters don't have the information; ballots exhaust them.
counterarguments.answer: California asks voters to absorb dozens of complex propositions at once. This platform asks few questions, one at a time, each with a plain-language context page wired into a cited document corpus — the information problem is the budget explorer's entire job. And the research is kinder to voters than the caricature: studies repeatedly find voter-competence fears overstated when information is accessible.

counterarguments.objection: Online participation just polls the comfortable.
counterarguments.answer: Correct — online alone is self-selection with a interface. That is why paper ballots at counters, text messaging, and kiosks are core channels, not accessibility garnish; why Lahti's library voting is a founding precedent; and why every result displays its tiers and channels honestly instead of claiming to be the county's voice.

counterarguments.objection: These platforms fade when their champions move on.
counterarguments.answer: Porto Alegre's erosion is the honest scar in the record. The mitigation is architectural: open source, one cheap server, county specifics isolated in a config file, steady-state operations designed for under three hours a week, a succession envelope written before it's needed, and a stated win condition of being absorbed by a better steward. Built to survive indifference, not to require enthusiasm.

closing: None of this requires anyone to lose an argument. It requires the trail to be visible, the questions to be askable, and the counting to be checkable. We think a county that has those three things makes better decisions than one that doesn't — and that is the entire platform, stated as a belief. Everything else on this site is evidence.
